extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners / attorneys subject to USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline (OED) investigations and discipline proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used to assess alleged professional misconduct by patent practitioners in USPTO/OED disciplinary investigations and proceedings (false statements, cooperation, client communications, record production).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the decision: preparing a statement the practitioner knew contained falsehoods for a client to sign and submitting it to OED; making false or misleading statements to a client about the status of patent matters. The decision treats deceitful half-truths or concealment of material facts as actual fraud (citing 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(d)). Case citations (e.g., In re Edelson) illustrate that providing false or misleading information to a client regarding pending matters can lead to suspension/exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule protects the integrity and procedural functioning of the judicial/disciplinary system and the work of disciplinary authorities. Prejudice may arise from multiple acts that cause some harm or from a single act causing substantial harm. Example: false statements that impede an OED investigation, leading to protracted investigation with multiple RFIs and witness interviews, are prejudicial to the administration of justice (the decision credits such conduct as violating 11.804(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(a) — Knowingly making a false statement of material fact in connection with a disciplinary matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation requires that the practitioner knowingly made a false statement of material fact in connection with a disciplinary matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements identified: (1) whether the practitioner made an assertion of material fact that was false; (2) whether the assertion was made knowing it was false; (3) whether the false assertion occurred in correspondence/statements to OED (e.g., Proposed Statement, responses to RFIs); and (4) whether the practitioner knew the statement was false when made. Examples: false assertions about a client's intent to abandon applications, about client payments, about assignment status, or about the obtainability of records. The decision applies a clear-and-convincing evidence standard when assessing knowledge and falsity and analyzes testimony and documentary evidence to determine knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) — Failure to cooperate in a disciplinary investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation occurs for failure to cooperate with OED’s investigation, including knowingly failing to respond to a lawful demand or failing to disclose facts necessary to correct a misapprehension known to have arisen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites a common definition of 'cooperate' ('to work with or act with another... willingly and agreeably') and observes that making false statements may constitute failure to cooperate but that the term is narrower. A practitioner must disclose facts necessary to correct misapprehensions within a 'reasonable time' (not necessarily immediate). Examples of failure: refusing to attempt to produce records within control, refusing to answer RFIs, asserting inquiries are 'unwarranted' or 'have no bearing.' Case law (e.g., In re Boyd, In re DeLuca) supports discipline for failure to produce client files/records.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a) — False statements to a tribunal (overlap with OED rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.303(a) prohibits knowingly making false statements of fact or law to a tribunal, failing to correct false statements previously made to the tribunal, offering evidence known to be false, or failing to take reasonable remedial measures once falsity is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats the elements as essentially the same as 11.801(a)/(b) but distinguishes scope: 11.303 governs disclosures to tribunals, while 11.801 governs disclosures in OED investigations. Where facts are alleged under both, the tribunal may prefer finding under the more specific rule (11.801) to avoid inflating gravity by duplicative findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness requirement for corrective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who knows a misapprehension has arisen must disclose the correcting fact within a reasonable time; the rule does not require 'immediate' disclosure but requires timeliness for the disclosure to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the case, the practitioner knew a client would not sign the Proposed Statement (creating a misapprehension) but did not inform OED until three months later in response to a specific RFI; the decision finds that delay constituted a failure to correct the misapprehension. The 'reasonable time' inquiry is fact-specific; an ongoing investigation does not excuse unreasonable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality — what facts are material in OED disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are material if they bear on the disciplinary matter under investigation (e.g., whether a client agreed to abandon applications, whether payments were made, status of assignments, whether records are reasonably obtainable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats statements about client intent to abandon, payment history toward legal fees, record location/availability, and assignment status as material because they affect the merits of the disciplinary allegations and the OED's investigation. Materiality informs whether false statements can sustain a violation under the cited rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge/proof standard for falsity and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove violations such as 11.801(a), the Director must show the practitioner knowingly made false statements; the tribunal assesses whether the practitioner knew the statements were false when made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies a 'clear and convincing' evidentiary standard to findings of knowledge and falsity. The tribunal examines contemporaneous documents, witness testimony, inconsistencies, and later admissions. The decision distinguishes statements the practitioner plausibly could have believed true (e.g., subjective client satisfaction) from statements proven to be known false at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable obtainability of records and attorney responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney is responsible for the organization and accessibility of his files, including records in storage; such records must be presumed reasonably obtainable, especially if only a few years old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision rejects arguments that disorganization or remote/uncomfortable storage conditions excuse failure to produce files. Purpose of storage is access; a practitioner cannot avoid production requests on the basis of his own disorganization or location choices. Failure to attempt to locate/produce records that are within the practitioner's control supports a finding of failure to cooperate or obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive half-truths or concealment constitute actual fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceitful statements of half-truths or concealment of material facts are treated as actual fraud under the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explicitly cites 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(d) and interprets certain misrepresentations (e.g., stating a client paid nothing toward fees when checks were issued) as deceitful half-truths. Such conduct is characterized as serious misconduct often leading to suspension or exclusion in other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties in representing co-clients and dual-representation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing co-clients, a practitioner must not ignore risks of divided interests and must confirm authority/communications with each co-client rather than relying solely on one client's representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds it misleading and a violation for an attorney to assert he had no authority to communicate with a co-client based solely on the other co-client's direction, or to fail to confirm assignment/authority. Maintaining business relationships does not excuse neglecting co-client interests; failure to investigate/confirm communications and authority can support violations of rules discussed above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to produce records or obstruction as failure to cooperate/prejudicial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to attempt to produce records within control, asserting records are 'not reasonably obtainable' without effort, or objecting that OED's inquiries have 'no bearing' can constitute failure to cooperate and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats such refusals as attempts to avoid producing responsive documents and as evidence of lack of respect for OED's investigation. Case law is cited where failure to produce client files or to respond appropriately resulted in discipline. The tribunal considers whether the practitioner actually attempted to locate files, whether the files were within his control, and whether asserted hardships are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding duplicative findings when rules overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same facts could support violations of multiple overlapping rules (e.g., 11.801(a)/(b) and 11.303(a) or 11.804(c)), the tribunal may find violation under the rule most specifically applicable to avoid inflating the gravity of the violations by duplicative findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains that Rule 11.303 governs disclosures to tribunals while Rule 11.801 governs disclosures in OED investigations (making 11.801 more specific here), and thus finds violation under 11.801(a)/(b) without separately finding a duplicative violation of 11.303(a) or 11.804(c) in some counts.
